q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Protonate the alkene so that the more stable carbocation forms, then let bromide bond to that carbon.
w: HBr adds by Markovnikov's rule. H+ bonds to the CH carbon of the C=C, which leaves the positive charge on the carbon bearing two methyl groups (a tertiary cation). Bromide traps that cation to give 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. Protonating the other alkene carbon would give a less stable secondary cation.
x: 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane places Br on the less substituted alkene carbon; that would require the secondary cation, not the tertiary one.
1-Bromo-2-methylbutane has Br on a CH<sub>2</sub> that was a methyl group, not one of the two alkene carbons.
1-Bromo-3-methylbutane puts Br on a primary carbon that was never part of the C=C; HBr adds only across the double bond.

q: What is the major product of this reaction? (Assume the carbocation rearranges whenever a more stable cation can form.)
h: Draw the first carbocation, then ask whether a neighboring hydrogen can shift to make a more stable one.
w: Protonation of the terminal CH2 gives a secondary cation at C2. The neighboring C3 carries a hydrogen and two methyls, so a 1,2-hydride shift converts the secondary cation into a tertiary cation. Chloride traps the tertiary cation: 2-chloro-2-methylbutane is the major product. The unrearranged 2-chloro-3-methylbutane forms only as a minor product.
x: 2-Chloro-3-methylbutane is the unrearranged Markovnikov product; it forms, but most of the secondary cation rearranges before chloride traps it.
1-Chloro-3-methylbutane is the anti-Markovnikov product; HCl adds through a carbocation, which never forms on the terminal carbon.
1-Chloro-2-methylbutane has Cl on a primary carbon; no step of the mechanism produces a primary cation there.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: The first carbocation sits next to a quaternary carbon. What can migrate from that carbon?
w: Protonation gives a secondary cation at C2, next to the quaternary C3 that has three methyls and no hydrogen. A 1,2-methyl shift moves one methyl (with its bonding pair) to C2 and leaves a tertiary cation on C3. Bromide traps it to give 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.
x: 3-Bromo-2,2-dimethylbutane is the unrearranged product; the secondary cation rearranges to the tertiary one faster than most of it is trapped.
1-Bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane is the anti-Markovnikov product, which needs radical conditions (HBr with peroxides).
1-Bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane has Br on a primary carbon; the methyl shift leaves the charge on a tertiary carbon, not a primary one.

q: Which species is the intermediate in this reaction?
h: HBr adds in two steps; the first step is protonation of the C=C.
w: Protonation of the CH carbon of 1-methylcyclohexene puts the positive charge on the ring carbon that carries the methyl, giving the tertiary 1-methylcyclohexyl cation. Bromide then adds to it to give 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.
x: The secondary cation forms only if H<sup>+</sup> adds to the methyl-bearing carbon, which is the less stable choice.
A bridged bromonium ion forms when Br<sub>2</sub> adds to an alkene; HBr adds H<sup>+</sup> first, not Br<sup>+</sup>.
A carbanion would need a nucleophile to add first; the alkene is the nucleophile here and H<sup>+</sup> is the electrophile.

q: What is the product of this two-step sequence? (Chiral products form as racemates; one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: Decide which carbon gets boron, then remember that H and B add to the same face and oxidation keeps the configuration.
w: BH3 adds in one concerted step: boron bonds to the less substituted alkene carbon (C2) and hydrogen to the methyl-bearing carbon (C1), both from the same face (syn). H2O2/NaOH replaces C–B with C–OH with retention. The new H on C1 and the OH on C2 are cis, so the methyl and OH are trans: trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, formed as a racemate.
x: cis-2-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol would require H and OH on opposite faces; hydroboration is syn and oxidation occurs with retention.
1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol is the Markovnikov alcohol from acid hydration or oxymercuration, not from hydroboration.
Cyclohexylmethanol would come from hydroboration of methylenecyclohexane, whose C=C is outside the ring.

q: What is the product of this reaction sequence?
h: Oxymercuration follows the same regiochemistry as acid hydration but without rearrangement.
w: Hg(OAc)2 forms a mercurinium ion; water opens it at the more substituted carbon (C2), and NaBH4 replaces the C–HgOAc bond with C–H. Net Markovnikov addition of H and OH: hexan-2-ol.
x: Hexan-1-ol is the anti-Markovnikov alcohol from hydroboration–oxidation.
Hexan-3-ol would need a hydride shift; the mercurinium ion does not rearrange, and a shift would only give another secondary cation anyway.
A 1,2-diol comes from dihydroxylation (OsO<sub>4</sub>); NaBH<sub>4</sub> puts H, not OH, where mercury was.

q: Which reagents carry out this conversion in good yield?
h: The target is the Markovnikov alcohol with the carbon skeleton unchanged. Which method avoids a free carbocation?
w: The target, 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, is the Markovnikov alcohol with no change to the skeleton. Oxymercuration–demercuration gives Markovnikov addition through a bridged mercurinium ion, so the methyl shift that plagues this substrate cannot occur.
x: Acid-catalyzed hydration goes through the secondary cation, which undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift and gives mainly 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.
Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov and gives the primary alcohol 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol.
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups and gives 3,3-dimethylbutane-1,2-diol, not a mono-alcohol.

q: What is the product? The two new stereocenters form as a racemate; one enantiomer is drawn.
h: Both alkene carbons are tertiary, so focus on stereochemistry: which two groups are delivered to the same face?
w: Hydroboration is a syn addition: H goes to one alkene carbon and B to the other from the same face, and oxidation replaces B with OH with retention. So the OH on C1 and the new H on C2 are cis. Each original methyl is pushed to the face opposite the group that added to its carbon: with OH up at C1, the C1 methyl is down; with H up at C2, the C2 methyl is down. The product is 1,2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol with the two methyl groups cis (OH trans to the C2 methyl).
x: This diastereomer has the two methyls trans, which would require H and OH to add to opposite faces (anti addition).
A cis-1,2-diol forms with OsO<sub>4</sub>; hydroboration–oxidation introduces only one OH.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane is the product of catalytic hydrogenation (H<sub>2</sub>, Pt), not hydroboration–oxidation.

q:
Which statements correctly explain why hydroboration–oxidation of propene gives propan-1-ol rather than propan-2-ol?
I. Boron, the electron-poor end of the B–H bond, bonds to the less substituted alkene carbon.
II. In the four-center transition state, partial positive charge builds on the more substituted carbon, which supports it better.
III. Putting the bulky boron group on the terminal CH2 minimizes steric strain.
IV. A secondary carbocation forms and is trapped by hydride from boron.
h: Hydroboration is concerted. Check each statement for both electronic and steric reasoning.
w: Statements I, II and III are all correct and work together: boron is the electrophile, it bonds to the terminal carbon, the slight δ+ in the transition state is on the secondary carbon, and the larger BH2 group goes to the less hindered carbon. Statement IV is false because hydroboration is concerted and has no carbocation intermediate. Answer: I, II and III only.
x: Statement II is also correct: the electronic preference (δ+ on the more substituted carbon) reinforces the steric one.
Statement IV is false; no carbocation forms, which is also why hydroboration never rearranges.
Statement IV is false, and statement I (boron as the electrophile bonding to the terminal carbon) is a key part of the explanation.

q: What is the major product of this reaction?
h: Draw the first carbocation and look at the carbon next to it. Is there a hydrogen on a more substituted neighbor?
w: Protonation of the terminal CH2 gives a secondary cation next to the ring CH. A 1,2-hydride shift from that ring carbon gives the tertiary 1-ethylcyclohexyl cation, and bromide traps it: 1-bromo-1-ethylcyclohexane.
x: (1-Bromoethyl)cyclohexane is the unrearranged product; the secondary cation shifts a hydride to reach a tertiary cation first.
(2-Bromoethyl)cyclohexane is anti-Markovnikov; it needs HBr with peroxides (a radical mechanism).
Ring expansion would give a secondary cycloheptyl cation, no better than the starting cation; the one-step hydride shift reaches a tertiary cation.

q: In the acid-catalyzed hydration of 2-methylpropene (H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>), which step is rate-determining?
c: Protonation of the alkene to form the tert-butyl cation
Attack of water on the tert-butyl cation
Deprotonation of the oxonium ion to give the alcohol
Simultaneous addition of H and OH in one concerted step
h: Which step creates a high-energy intermediate from a neutral, stable starting material?
w: The slow step is protonation of the alkene: it breaks the π bond and creates a carbocation. Water capturing the cation and the final proton transfer are both fast.
x: Water attack on a carbocation is a fast combination of a nucleophile with a reactive cation.
Proton transfer from the oxonium ion to water is fast and nearly thermoneutral.
Acid-catalyzed hydration is stepwise through a carbocation; it is not a concerted addition.

q: For which alkene do acid-catalyzed hydration and hydroboration–oxidation give the same constitutional isomer of the alcohol?
h: Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov products are the same only if the two alkene carbons are equivalent and no rearrangement is possible.
w: In cyclohexene the two alkene carbons are equivalent, so Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov addition both give cyclohexanol, and the secondary cyclohexyl cation has no better cation to shift to.
x: 1-Methylcyclohexene gives 1-methylcyclohexanol by acid hydration but trans-2-methylcyclohexanol by hydroboration.
Methylenecyclohexane gives 1-methylcyclohexanol by acid hydration but cyclohexylmethanol by hydroboration.
3-Methylbut-1-ene gives 2-methylbutan-2-ol (after a hydride shift) by acid hydration but 3-methylbutan-1-ol by hydroboration.

q:
Which statements about oxymercuration–demercuration (1. Hg(OAc)2, H2O 2. NaBH4) are correct?
I. A bridged mercurinium ion forms, so carbocation rearrangements do not occur.
II. Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the mercurinium ion.
III. NaBH4 replaces the C–HgOAc bond with a C–H bond.
IV. The H and OH are always added syn to each other.
h: Think separately about the oxymercuration step (stereospecific) and the demercuration step.
w: I, II and III are correct. The mercurinium ion has no free carbocation, so no shifts; water opens it at the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov); NaBH4 replaces mercury with hydrogen. Statement IV is false: the demercuration step goes through a radical and is not stereospecific, so the overall addition of H and OH is not reliably syn or anti. Answer: I, II and III only.
x: Statement IV is false (demercuration is not stereospecific), and II and III are true.
Statement I is also true; the bridged ion is exactly why this method avoids rearrangement.
Statement IV is false; replacing Hg with H goes through a radical, so the H can end up on either face.

q: What is the major product of this sequence?
h: The solvent is the nucleophile that opens the mercurinium ion.
w: Hg(OAc)2 forms the mercurinium ion; the solvent, methanol, attacks the more substituted carbon (the one bearing the methyl). NaBH4 then replaces mercury with H. The result is Markovnikov addition of H and OCH3: 1-methoxy-1-methylcyclohexane.
x: 1-Methoxy-2-methylcyclohexane has OCH<sub>3</sub> on the less substituted carbon; the nucleophile opens the mercurinium ion at the more substituted carbon.
1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol would form if water were the solvent; here methanol is the nucleophile.
(Methoxymethyl)cyclohexane puts OCH<sub>3</sub> on a carbon that was not part of the C=C.

q: Hydroboration–oxidation (1. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  2. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH) of which alkene gives racemic trans-2-methylcyclopentan-1-ol (shown) as the only constitutional isomer?
h: Work backward: OH marks where boron went; the H added to the neighboring carbon, which carries the methyl.
w: Boron (and later OH) goes to the less substituted alkene carbon, and H goes to the other carbon, syn. For the OH to sit next to the methyl-bearing carbon, the C=C must join those two carbons: 1-methylcyclopentene. Syn addition puts H and OH cis, so methyl and OH are trans, as in the target.
x: Methylenecyclopentane gives cyclopentylmethanol; the OH ends up on the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub>.
3-Methylcyclopentene has two similar secondary alkene carbons, so boron adds to both and gives a mixture of 2- and 3-methylcyclopentanols.
4-Methylcyclopentene gives only 3-methylcyclopentan-1-ol; its OH is two carbons from the methyl.

q: What is the major product when 2-methylpropene is treated with H<sub>2</sub>O and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
h: Which carbocation forms when the alkene is protonated?
w: Protonation of the CH2 carbon gives the tert-butyl cation; water adds and loses a proton to give 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol), the Markovnikov product.
x: 2-Methylpropan-1-ol is the anti-Markovnikov alcohol from hydroboration–oxidation.
A diol needs a dihydroxylation reagent such as OsO<sub>4</sub>; aqueous acid adds only H and OH.
2-Methylpropane would require H<sub>2</sub> and a metal catalyst; water adds OH, not H.

q: (R)-3-Methylhex-1-ene is treated with H2O and catalytic H2SO4. Which best describes the major product?
c: 3-Methylhexan-3-ol, formed as a single enantiomer because C3 keeps its configuration
3-Methylhexan-2-ol, formed as a mixture of diastereomers
h: Follow the carbocation: does it rearrange, and what happens to the original stereocenter?
w: Protonation gives a secondary cation at C2. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 (the stereocenter) gives the more stable tertiary cation at C3, which is planar, so the original configuration is lost. Water attacks either face equally, giving 3-methylhexan-3-ol as a racemic mixture (C3 bears CH3, ethyl, propyl and OH, so it is a stereocenter).
x: C3 becomes the sp<sup>2</sup> cation carbon after the hydride shift, so its configuration cannot be retained.
3-Methylhexan-2-ol is the unrearranged product; the secondary cation shifts a hydride to reach the tertiary cation.
The primary alcohol is the hydroboration product; acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov.

q:
Rank these alkenes by rate of acid-catalyzed hydration (slowest to fastest).
I. ethene II. propene III. 2-methylpropene
h: The rate-determining step forms a carbocation. Apply the Hammond postulate.
w: Protonation is rate-determining and its transition state resembles the carbocation. Ethene gives a primary cation, propene a secondary, and 2-methylpropene a tertiary cation, so the rate order is I < II < III.
x: This reverses the order; more substituted cations form faster, not slower.
Ethene cannot be faster than propene: it would have to form a primary (essentially methyl-like) cation.
2-Methylpropene forms the tertiary cation, so it reacts fastest, not in the middle.
